title: New Tools Give Parents Three Ways to Shield Infants From RSV
excerpt: With two monoclonal antibodies and a maternal vaccine now available, doctors say the 2026 RSV season offers the strongest infant protection ever against the leading cause of hospitalization in babies.
body:
• Three FDA-approved options now protect infants from severe RSV: nirsevimab (Beyfortus), clesrovimab (Enflonsia), and the maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo)
  • Real-world data from Great Britain shows a 50 percent drop in newborn ICU admissions in the first full year of the maternal RSV vaccination program
  • RSV season runs from November through March, and doctors recommend parents discuss protection options with their pediatrician before fall

For parents preparing for the upcoming respiratory season, the landscape for protecting infants from respiratory syncytial virus has changed dramatically. RSV, the leading cause of hospitalization in babies under one year old, now has three FDA-approved preventive tools, giving families and pediatricians more choices than ever before.

The Three Lines of Defense

The current arsenal includes two monoclonal antibodies, nirsevimab (Beyfortus, by AstraZeneca and Sanofi) and clesrovimab (Enflonsia, by Merck), plus a maternal vaccine from Pfizer called Abrysvo. The CDC recommends all infants receive protection through either a maternal vaccine during pregnancy or one of the monoclonal antibodies, according to its updated clinical guidance.

Nirsevimab was the first breakthrough, approved in 2023 for infants younger than eight months entering their first RSV season. The CDC also recommends it for children aged eight to 19 months at increased risk during their second RSV season. Clesrovimab received FDA approval in June 2025, based on data from the CLEVER and SMART clinical trials showing that a single dose significantly reduced RSV-related hospitalizations over a five-month period.

"Now we move to a totally different era. We have two monoclonal antibodies, nirsevimab and now clesrovimab, as well as a maternal vaccine, that are all indicated to prevent RSV disease during the first season."

— Dr. Octavio Ramilo, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital

How They Differ

While both monoclonal antibodies provide passive immunity, meaning they supply ready-made antibodies rather than teaching the infant's immune system, they work through different mechanisms. Clesrovimab targets a different site on the RSV protein called site four, which is present in both pre-fusion and post-fusion forms of the virus. It also uses a single fixed dose regardless of the infant's weight, simplifying administration, according to Dr. Ramilo.

The maternal vaccine works differently. When given to pregnant women between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation, Abrysvo stimulates the mother's immune system to produce antibodies that cross the placenta and protect the baby from birth. A phase 4 study published in Pediatrics found that both maternal vaccination and infant immunization produce strong increases in neutralizing antibody levels.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends either maternal vaccination or an infant monoclonal antibody. Most infants do not need both, though certain high-risk cases, such as premature babies or those born shortly after vaccination, may benefit from a combined approach.

Real-World Results

Early data from countries that have rolled out RSV prevention programs are encouraging. Great Britain reported a 50 percent reduction in newborn ICU admissions during the first full year of its maternal RSV vaccination program. In the United States, the CDC estimates that 58,000 to 80,000 children under five are hospitalized due to RSV infection each year, and two seasons of real-world data show that prevention significantly reduces both hospitalizations and outpatient visits.

Dr. Ramilo highlighted the potential long-term benefits of early RSV protection. "Data suggests that if babies get infected in the first six months of life, the likelihood of having more recurrent respiratory infections is much higher," he said. "Maybe we can not only prevent the acute events but have a potential long-term benefit in preventing diseases like wheezing or even asthma."

What Parents Should Do Now

RSV season in the United States typically runs from November through March, and doctors urge parents to discuss their options with a pediatrician before fall. Parents of infants at higher risk, including premature babies, those with chronic lung disease or congenital heart conditions, should be especially proactive.

Basic prevention measures complement immunization: frequent handwashing, keeping sick family members away from newborns, cleaning high-touch surfaces and using a humidifier to ease congestion. For parents in India, the RSV prevention landscape is evolving as well, though access to the newer monoclonal antibodies may vary by region and availability.

For the first time, parents have real choices for protecting their babies from one of childhood's most dangerous infections. The science has caught up, and the tools are here.
